## FINAL HYPOTHESIS

**In the 1989 NLSY79 cross-section the likelihood of dissaving falls with age — roughly −0.5 percentage points per year, about −4.3 pp from age 24 to age 32 — and the decline is essentially linear, not U-shaped or inverted-U; but this age gradient is not a general life-cycle effect. It is concentrated entirely in the respondents whose INCOME equals the constant 47.279 (inferred mean-imputed missing income), while respondents with genuinely reported income show no detectable age gradient at all. So the hypothesis must be stated conditionally: among NLSY79 respondents aged 24–32 in 1989, older age is associated with a lower probability of net dissaving, and that association is driven by — and only statistically reliable within — the ~31% of the sample carrying the constant mean-imputed income value.**

## Results that produced it (all from `python analysis.py`, logit, complete cases — the file has zero missing cells)

**1. Primary spec (full sample, n = 12,686; DISSAVED ~ AGE_C + AGE_C2 + GENDER + log(1+INCOME) + BLACK + HISPANIC + INCOME_MEANIMPUTED):**
- AGE_C −0.0323 (p = 0.0008), AGE_C2 −0.0042 (p = 0.347); joint age LR = 11.81, df 2, p = 0.0027. VIFs 1.03 / 1.01 (centring killed the r = 0.999 AGE/AGE_2 collinearity).
- AME on age: −0.55 pp/yr (quadratic spec), −0.53 pp/yr (linear); per-year OR 0.969 (95% CI 0.951–0.987).
- Predicted P(DISSAVED) at covariate means: 23.3% (24), 23.0 (26), 22.1 (28), 20.7 (30), 18.8% (32) [quadratic]; 23.95 → 19.67% in the linear spec, change **−4.28 pp, 95% CI −6.81 to −1.75**, bootstrap (150 reps) mean −4.21, CI −6.59 to −1.49.

**2. Shape — tests picked the language, and they reject the inverted-U:**
- LR quadratic|covariates = 0.887, df 1, **p = 0.346** (AIC prefers linear 13109.3 vs 13110.4).
- Turning point = **age 24.0 (95% CI 15.9–32.1)** → pinned at the left edge of support, unidentifiable; curvature must be called interior-only, not a peak.
- Factor-age vs quadratic | covariates: LR = 4.296, df 6, p = 0.637 (quadratic adequate, adds nothing).
- Unadjusted only: LR = 4.759, p = 0.029, max at 25.5 (CI 23.3–27.8). In the drop sample the quadratic is null (p = 0.58/0.69). So: "declines with age across mid-20s→early 30s", monotone; the 26–27 bump in the raw series is noise.

**3. Decisive robustness — pre-committed drop of the imputed-income rows (n = 8,723): the effect disappears.**
- Joint age LR = 0.181, df 2, **p = 0.913**; AGE_C = −0.0020 (p = 0.85); predicted 28.9% (24) → 28.6% (32), −0.26 pp (95% CI −3.66 to +3.14; bootstrap −0.07, CI −3.12 to +3.03).
- Age × income-group interaction: **LR = 40.83, df 1, p = 1.7e-10**; per-year logit slope −0.0016 (p = 0.88) for genuine income vs **−0.155 (SE 0.022, OR 0.856/yr)** for the imputed group, whose predicted rate falls 16.5% → 5.1% (−11.4 pp).
- Composition decomposition: raw 24-25→30-32 change −4.00 pp; standardising the imputed share to the sample-wide 31.24% leaves −1.76 pp ⇒ **56% of the raw gradient is composition** (imputed share rises 27.1→24.1→32.5→38.9% across bins while their own rate falls 15.6→16.8→10.1→7.0%).
- Direction does not flip sign, it attenuates to null — so per your instruction the headline is stated conditionally, not by picking the convenient sample.

**4. Mechanism (3-state table; DISSAVED and SAMESAVE never both 1 — 0 such rows; both 0 = 4,913 net savers).** Net savers rise 30.9 / 32.0 / 39.0 / 49.5% and "same or no savings" fall 44.4 / 42.0 / 37.4 / 29.8% across the four age bins: the age decline in dissaving is mostly a shift into positive saving.

**5. Covariates / sensitivities.** log(1+INCOME) +0.331 (OR 1.39, p ≈ 1e-39) with AME +5.6 pp *controlling the imputed indicator*, though unadjusted income terciles are non-monotone (23.5 / 28.7 / 18.5%); income-tercile spec leaves age unchanged (AGE_C −0.031, p = 0.0014). INCOME_MEANIMPUTED OR 0.248 (AME −23.7 pp). Male OR 0.864 (AME −2.5 pp), BLACK OR 1.42 (+5.9 pp), HISPANIC OR 1.16 (+2.4 pp). Age×gender interactions ns (p = 0.79, 0.72). LPM (HC1) reproduces age −0.0051 (p = 0.0014) with AGE_C2 p = 0.42.

## Variable-relation list (results/relations.csv, 12 rows)
AGE→DISSAVED negative ≈linear; AGE_2 concavity unsupported (turning point at support edge); AGE→DISSAVED null in genuine-income sample; AGE×income-group interaction decisive; INCOME→DISSAVED positive conditional / non-monotone unconditional; INCOME_MEANIMPUTED→DISSAVED strongly negative; GENDER (male lower), BLACK (higher), HISPANIC (higher); AGE→SAMESAVE/net-saving shift; **AGE↔AGE_2 exact functional dependency (AGE_2 = AGE², r = 0.999, zero independent information)**; **DISSAVED↔SAMESAVE mutually exclusive indicators of one 3-state outcome**.

## Limitations
Single 1989 cross-section of one cohort, **ages 24–32 only** (3% at age 32): age is inseparable from cohort/life stage, and no claim transfers outside 24–32 — nothing here speaks to dissaving later in life. Strictly associational: no marriage, children, education, employment, wealth or debt controls exist in the file. The reading of the 47.279 mass as mean-imputed missingness is an inference from exact arithmetic (it equals the mean of all other rows) and remains undocumented — the conditional form of the hypothesis is what insulates it from that uncertainty. INCOME units unverified; 131 exact zeros treated as real; 167 rows at the max look top-coded and winsorising is vacuous (q99 = max), hence log1p. BMI excluded from the primary model by design (max 176 kg/m², out of scope). Bootstrap intervals use 150 replications, so the outer CI endpoints are themselves Monte-Carlo noisy (±~0.2 pp).

payload.hypothesis: In the 1989 NLSY79 cross-section (respondents aged 24-32 only, n = 12,686), the probability of net dissaving (DISSAVED = 1) declines with age - about -0.5 percentage points per year, from roughly 24% at age 24 to 19.7% at age 32, a total of -4.3 pp (95% CI -6.8 to -1.8) after adjusting for GENDER, log income, BLACK, HISPANIC and an indicator for mean-imputed income - and the decline is essentially linear rather than U-shaped or inverted-U (the AGE_2 term is not supported conditional on covariates, LR p = 0.35, and its implied turning point, age 24.0 with CI 15.9-32.1, lies at the edge of the observed support). Crucially, this age gradient is not a general life-cycle effect: dropping the 31% of rows whose INCOME equals the constant 47.279 (inferred mean-imputed missing income) removes it entirely (joint age LR p = 0.91; predicted 28.9% at 24 vs 28.6% at 32, change -0.26 pp, 95% CI -3.7 to +3.1), and an age x income-group interaction is decisive (LR = 40.8, p = 1.7e-10), with a per-year logit slope of -0.0016 (p = 0.88) among respondents with genuinely reported income versus -0.155 (OR 0.856/year) in the imputed-income group (16.5% -> 5.1% from 24 to 32). About 56% of the raw -4.0 pp gradient is compositional, since the share of imputed-income respondents rises from 27% to 39% with age while their own dissaving rate falls from 16% to 7%. Descriptively, the age decline is a shift out of 'savings unchanged / no savings' (44% -> 30%) and into positive saving (31% -> 50%), since DISSAVED and SAMESAVE are mutually exclusive states of one three-outcome. All statements are associational, confined to ages 24-32 in a single 1989 cross-section, and non-causal; the effect of age in this file should be described as a modest, monotone, covariate-adjusted decline that is statistically reliable only within the mean-imputed-income subgroup.
payload.workflow: Single reproducible script analysis.py (python analysis.py; runs in ~20 s, no network, statsmodels/scipy/pandas only) writes results/model_report.txt (full log), results/relations.csv and pairs with results/hypothesis.md. Steps: (1) load data/nls_bmi_processed.csv, report shape/dtypes/missingness/binary levels/distributions; (2) derive GEND_M, INCOME_MEANIMPUTED (INCOME == 47.279064), INCOME_LOG = log1p(INCOME) (winsorising vacuous because q99 = max), centred AGE_C = AGE - 27.857 and AGE_C2 to defuse the AGE/AGE_2 collinearity, income terciles, and a 3-state savings status; (3) descriptive dissaving rates by single year of age and by coarse bins plus the 3-state composition table and the rate by age bin x income group; (4) nested logits M1 (linear age), M2 (centred quadratic), M3L (linear + covariates), M3 primary (quadratic + covariates + imputed indicator), M4/M4f (factor-in-age), M5 (income terciles), M6 (age x gender), fitted pre-committed on both the full sample (primary) and the sample excluding imputed-income rows (decisive robustness); (5) LR tests for the quadratic and for factor-vs-quadratic adequacy, joint age tests, VIFs; (6) predicted P(DISSAVED) at ages 24/26/28/30/32 with delta-method 95% CIs, average and per-year marginal effects, quadratic turning point with delta-method interval, and the 24->32 endpoint change with delta-method and 150-replication nonparametric bootstrap CIs; (7) composition decomposition standardising the imputed-income share and the formal age x income-group interaction test; (8) LPM (HC1) and income-tercile sensitivities; (9) machine-readable relation summary and the written hypothesis.
